title: What an angle is, measured in degrees
definition: Stand at a corner and open a pair of scissors: the two blades share a point, and how far they have swung apart is the angle. We measure that swing in degrees — one full spin sliced into 360 tiny wedges. A protractor is a ruler bent into a half-circle that counts the wedges for you.

slides.narration: What an angle is, measured in degrees

slides.caption: Two blades share one corner and swing apart — how wide is the gap?
slides.narration: How wide is the swing? Freeze-frame two blades opening from a single locked corner. Their tips race apart — but how far did they actually swing? That mystery gap is what we want to pin down.

slides.caption: That gap between the blades has a name: the angle.
slides.narration: That gap between the blades has a special name: the angle. Look at the little green wedge drawn between them — that green shape is the angle itself. But how do we measure a swing?

slides.caption: One full turn is sliced into 360 tiny wedges called degrees.
slides.narration: Here is the wild trick: take one perfect full turn around the corner and chop it into 360 tiny steps called degrees — a whole spin sliced like a pizza into 360 microscopic wedges, one skinny wedge per degree.

slides.caption: The swing fills 50 wedges — so the angle is 50 degrees.
slides.narration: Now count. The swing fills exactly fifty of those pizza wedges — so we call it fifty degrees. Not a made-up number; just how many wedges fit the gap.

slides.caption: A protractor is a half-circle of wedges that counts them for you.
slides.narration: Counting fifty wedges by hand would take forever, so we use a protractor — a ruler bent into a half-circle with the wedges marked on the rim. Line one blade up with zero, read where the other blade points: fifty.

slides.caption: Two lines from one shared corner — angles are everywhere.
slides.narration: Once you know what to look for, these wedge-angles are everywhere. The square corner of a book? Exactly ninety degrees. Ramps, clock hands, open scissors — every one is just two lines swinging apart from a shared corner.
